steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for our paper on MAS, a method that generates 3D motion using a diffusion model trained only on 2D motion from videos. Motivate the 3D data bottleneck, contrast with pose-estimation-based approaches, explain how the sampling works, and describe the domains we demonstrate it on.

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
3D motion generation is a field that is getting more and more popular, and it has important applications in computer-animated films, video games, virtual reality and more. One of the main bottlenecks of the current approaches is that they rely on 3D data. This data is usually acquired by actors in motion capture studios or created by professional animation artists. Both ways of getting data are costly and not scalable, they do not capture in-the-wild behavior, and they leave whole motion domains under-explored.

Luckily, video cameras are everywhere, so there are countless high-quality recordings of many different motions. A naive way to use these videos for motion generation would be to extract 3D pose estimations and use them as training data. But pose estimation methods are mostly trained with 3D data, so they inherit the same data limitations. Some methods need only 2D data, but they have noticeable artifacts and temporal inconsistencies.

Recently, two works used 3D motions estimated from images or videos in motion synthesis applications. The first one used them to enrich an existing motion capture dataset, and the second one used them as reference motions while learning a physically-based Reinforcement Learning policy. In both cases the quality issues were bridged with strong priors (either high-quality 3D data or physical simulation), so they stay limited to specific settings. Unlike the pose estimation approaches, we focus on unconditional 3D motion generation from pure noise.

- MAS
  - Multi-view Ancestral Sampling: diffusion-based 3D motion generation, needs only 2D motion data, can come only from videos
  - learn 2D motion diffusion model from videos -> MAS samples 3D motions from it
  - based on Ancestral Sampling (standard denoising loop); denoise multiple 2D views of one 3D motion simultaneously
  - every step: triangulate views into single 3D motion, project back -> multi-view consistency while following prior
  - project 3D noise to each view whenever sampling from a Gaussian
- Results / domains
  - diverse, realistic motions; 2D prior trained only on in-the-wild videos
  - a few seconds per 3D motion on a single standard GPU
  - mocap impractical, video abundant (Figure 1); off-the-shelf 2D pose estimators for training data
  - NBA basketball, horses (equestrian contests), rhythmic ball gymnastics with ball location
  - previously under-explored domains (3D data scarcity)

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
3D motion generation is a field that is getting more and more popular, and it has important applications in computer-animated films, video games, virtual reality and more. One of the main bottlenecks of the current approaches is that they rely on 3D data. This data is usually acquired by actors in motion capture studios or created by professional animation artists. Both ways of getting data are costly and not scalable, they do not capture in-the-wild behavior, and they leave whole motion domains under-explored.

Luckily, video cameras are everywhere, so there are countless high-quality recordings of many different motions. A naive way to use these videos for motion generation would be to extract 3D pose estimations and use them as training data. But pose estimation methods are mostly trained with 3D data, so they inherit the same data limitations. Some methods need only 2D data, but they have noticeable artifacts and temporal inconsistencies.

Recently, two works used 3D motions estimated from images or videos in motion synthesis applications. The first one used them to enrich an existing motion capture dataset, and the second one used them as reference motions while learning a physically-based Reinforcement Learning policy. In both cases the quality issues were bridged with strong priors (either high-quality 3D data or physical simulation), so they stay limited to specific settings. Unlike the pose estimation approaches, we focus on unconditional 3D motion generation from pure noise.

In this paper we present Multi-view Ancestral Sampling (MAS). MAS is a diffusion-based 3D motion generation method that only needs 2D motion data, which can be acquired only from videos. First we learn a 2D motion diffusion model from a set of videos, and then we use the MAS algorithm to sample 3D motions from this learned model. The method is based on Ancestral Sampling, which is the standard denoising loop for sampling from a diffusion model. MAS extends this and generates a 3D motion by denoising multiple 2D views that describe it at the same time. At each denoising step, all the views are triangulated into one 3D motion, and then this motion is projected back to each view. This keeps the views consistent with each other during the whole denoising process, and it still follows the predictions of the prior. To encourage multi-view consistency even more, whenever the 2D ancestral sampling process samples from a Gaussian distribution, we project a 3D noise to each view.

We show that MAS generates diverse and realistic motions from the underlying 3D motion distribution, using a 2D diffusion model trained only on motions from in-the-wild videos. We also show that because it relies on ancestral sampling, MAS can generate a 3D motion in only a few seconds on a single standard GPU. MAS is best in cases where getting 3D motion capture data is impractical but there is a lot of video footage (See Figure 1). In these cases we use off-the-shelf 2D pose estimators to extract 2D motion sequences from the video frames, and we train our diffusion prior on them. We demonstrate MAS in three domains: (1) motions of professional basketball players extracted from common NBA match recordings, (2) horse motions extracted from equestrian contests, and (3) human-ball interactions extracted from rhythmic ball gymnastics performances (the ball location is an extra parameter predicted by the model). These datasets show motion domains that were under-explored before because of 3D data scarcity.

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
3D motion generation is an increasingly popular field with prominent applications in computer-animated films, video games, virtual reality, and more. One of the main bottlenecks of current approaches is their reliance on 3D data, which is typically acquired by actors in motion capture studios or created by professional animation artists. Both forms of data acquisition are costly and not scalable, do not capture in-the-wild behavior, and leave entire motion domains under-explored.

Fortunately, the ubiquity of video cameras has led to countless high-quality recordings of a wide variety of motions. Naively, one way to leverage these videos for motion generation is to extract 3D pose estimations and use them as training data. However, pose estimation methods are mostly trained using 3D data [1,2], and thus inherit the same data limitations. Some methods only require 2D data [3,4], but they suffer from noticeable artifacts and temporal inconsistencies.

Recently, [5] and [6] incorporated 3D motions estimated from images or videos into motion synthesis applications. The former used them to enrich an existing motion capture dataset, and the latter used them as reference motions while learning a physically-based Reinforcement Learning policy. In both cases, the quality issues were bridged using strong priors (either high-quality 3D data or physical simulation), so these approaches remain limited to specific settings. In contrast to the pose estimation approaches, we focus on unconditional 3D motion generation from pure noise.

In this paper, we present Multi-view Ancestral Sampling (MAS), a diffusion-based 3D motion generation method that requires only 2D motion data, which can be acquired exclusively from videos. We first learn a 2D motion diffusion model from a set of videos, and then employ the MAS algorithm to sample 3D motions from this learned model. Our method builds on Ancestral Sampling, the standard denoising loop used for sampling from a diffusion model. MAS extends this concept, generating a 3D motion by simultaneously denoising multiple 2D views that describe it. At each denoising step, all views are triangulated into a single 3D motion, which is then projected back to each view. This ensures multi-view consistency throughout the denoising process while adhering to the prior's predictions. We further encourage multi-view consistency by projecting a 3D noise to each view whenever the 2D ancestral sampling process samples from a Gaussian distribution.

We show that MAS generates diverse and realistic motions from the underlying 3D motion distribution, using a 2D diffusion model trained exclusively on motions obtained from in-the-wild videos. Furthermore, we show that relying on ancestral sampling allows MAS to generate a 3D motion in only a few seconds on a single standard GPU. MAS excels in scenarios where acquiring 3D motion capture data is impractical but video footage is abundant (See Figure 1). In such settings, we apply off-the-shelf 2D pose estimators to extract 2D motion sequences from video frames and use them to train our diffusion prior. We demonstrate MAS in three domains: (1) professional basketball player motions extracted from common NBA match recordings, (2) horse motions extracted from equestrian contests, and (3) human-ball interactions extracted from rhythmic ball gymnastics performances (the ball location is an additional parameter predicted by the model). These datasets represent motion domains that were previously under-explored due to 3D data scarcity.

References:
[1] Muhammed Kocabas, Nikos Athanasiou, and Michael J Black. Vibe: Video inference for human body pose and shape estimation. In CVPR , 2020.
[2] Karthik Shetty, Annette Birkhold, Srikrishna Jaganathan, Norbert Strobel, Markus Kowarschik, Andreas Maier, and Bernhard Egger. Pliks: A pseudo-linear inverse kinematic solver for 3d human body estimation, 2023.
[3] Bastian Wandt, James J. Little, and Helge Rhodin. Elepose: Unsupervised 3d human pose estimation by predicting camera elevation and learning normalizing flows on 2d poses, 2021.
[4] Yicheng Deng, Cheng Sun, Jiahui Zhu, and Yongqi Sun. Svmac: Unsupervised 3d human pose estimation from a single image with single-view-multi-angle consistency, 2022.
[5] Samaneh Azadi, Akbar Shah, Thomas Hayes, Devi Parikh, and Sonal Gupta. Make-an-animation: Large-scale text-conditional 3d human motion generation, 2023.
[6] Haotian Zhang, Ye Yuan, Viktor Makoviychuk, Yunrong Guo, Sanja Fidler, Xue Bin Peng, and Kayvon Fatahalian. Learning physically simulated tennis skills from broadcast videos. ACM Trans. Graph. , 2023.
